records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Ornamental Onion, Persian Onion, Star of Persia), so Star of Persia is not first in it, and NC State's Description uses Star of Persia in running text. RHS's plant profile renders star of Persia as the common name beneath its H1 and MoBot's prose says commonly called star of Persia, so Star of Persia is the common name. Persian Onion, the second entry on NC State's list, is the name this catalog already files Allium hollandicum under. NC State lists Allium albopilosum as a previous name and RHS lists Allium albopilosum and Allium bodeanum as synonyms, so these belong to this one record. MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose spells the binomial Allium christophii (with an h).
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, dedicated page for Allium cristophii. The poison fields come from NC State's Poisonous to Humans block, which is human-scoped. Page lead: 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Poison Severity: Low (from the Poisonous to Humans block, not a cat or dog rating). Poison Symptoms: 'Symptoms may include: nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.' Poison Toxic Principle: Sulfides. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part field lists: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Co-listed tags and traits on the same page: Plant Type: Bulb, Poisonous; Problems: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs; Resistance To Challenges: Deer, Drought, Rabbits; page tags include #poisonous. The Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags are separate from the human-scoped block; the page gives no cat- or dog-specific symptom list, severity or dose. No handling warning is stated. Edibility field (same page): 'Bulbs and stems are edible raw or cooked. However, the plant also has poisonous characteristics as noted in the "Poisonous to Humans" section of this record.' It adds: 'Toxicity can depend on the age of the person or animal, the age of the plant, the part of the plant ingested, how much is ingested, whether the person or animal has sensitivities or allergies, whether it's eaten raw or cooked, and so forth.' It closes: 'Consult with a medical professional for further details.' No preparation times or conditions are given. Note the tension on the page itself: stems are called edible while Stems are also in the Poison Part list. MoBot and RHS pages state nothing about toxicity or edibility.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets is true only on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags; the page gives no cat- or dog-specific symptoms, severity or dose, and MoBot and RHS are silent on toxicity.

is_edible is true on NC State's Edibility field (bulbs and stems edible raw or cooked) but the same page rates the whole plant poisonous (Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems) and gives no preparation times; the page itself is internally in tension about stems. MoBot and RHS do not address eating.

outdoor_sun_exposure lists only full_sun: NC State's Light field, RHS Position and MoBot's Culture sentence all say full sun; NC State's Description also says 'full sun to partial shade' in its planting sentence, which is not added because the structured fields of all three sources exclude shade.

soil_drainage left null: NC State says well-drained soils, RHS says 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' and MoBot says dry to medium moisture, well-drained loams; bare well-drained is ambiguous and the sources do not agree on a clear scale position.

water_regime left null: MoBot Water field reads Dry to medium and NC State says it tolerates summer drought but requires moisture during the growing season; neither is a clear watering instruction mapping to one enum value.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: RHS pH field lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral (no bound); NC State and MoBot give no pH.

RHS Max Height and Max Spread read 0.1-0.5 metres, which conflicts with its own prose (to 60cm tall) and with NC State and MoBot; sizes use NC State's Dimensions block (Height 6-24 in, Width 12-24 in). MoBot says height 1.00 to 2.00 feet and spread 0.50 to 1.50 feet.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, chill damage, fertilizer and watering intervals are not given by any admissible source for this species; hardiness (NC State zones 4a-8b, RHS H5, MoBot zone 4 to 8) is not a damage-onset temperature.
Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA were not checked for a dedicated Allium cristophii page; none was found in the sources consulted.
MoBot lists Attracts: Butterflies and NC State lists Attracts: Pollinators and Songbirds; RHS carries the Plants for pollinators tag.

records.name_note: RHS's profile for Narcissus jonquilla (13) gives 'jonquil' as its common name, with 'common jonquil, lily of Mary' under Other common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list for this taxon reads Daffodil, Jonquil, Narcissus, Species Daffodil (leading with Daffodil), and its description prose calls the plant 'The Jonquil'. Jonquil is used as the common name. The bare name Daffodil is not used for this species because this catalog already files Narcissus pseudonarcissus as Daffodil.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Poisonous to Humans block, human-scoped): Poison Severity: Low (the page also states "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."). Poison Symptoms as the page words them: "Vomiting, salvation, diarrhea; large ingestions cause convulsions, low blood pressure, tremors, and cardiac arrhythmias. Bulbs are the most poisonous part." Poison Toxic Principle: Lycorine and other alkaloids. The page lists Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Separately from that human-scoped block, NC State's Problems field carries three tags: Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses; the page gives no ASPCA-style symptom list for those animals. Plant-type traits shown on the same page: Plant Type Bulb and Herbaceous Perennial. The severe signs (convulsions, low blood pressure, tremors, arrhythmias) are tied by NC State to large ingestions only, and bulbs are the most poisonous part. RHS (Potentially harmful field): "Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and for pets "Pets (dogs, cats, tortoises): Harmful if eaten; skin irritant." The two admissible sources differ on skin contact: RHS says skin irritant with a gloves warning, NC State says Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. ASPCA is not an admissible domain, so no ASPCA cat/dog/horse scoping is recorded. NC State's Poison block has no Poison Part row; its symptom text is the only part statement (bulbs most poisonous).
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden's page for Narcissus jonquilla (taxonid=275814) could not be loaded (connection error from qc.py/fetch), so MoBot is not cited; no other admissible source (Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD, UGA) was found with a dedicated page for this species.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture; NC State (Plant Type Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial; USDA zones 4a-8b) and RHS describe it as an outdoor bulb planted in the ground in fall.

water_regime left null: NC State gives only a soil adjective (Moist) and says the plant is tolerant of drought and heat but intolerant of extremely wet conditions; RHS's 'constantly moist during the growing season' is a Cultivation-paragraph soil preference that points to the shared daffodil guide (it says 'See daffodil cultivation for further advice'), so it is treated as genus boilerplate. No watering statement specific to this species was found. water_dry_down_target and the day-interval fields are null because this is an in-ground bulb and no source frames watering that way.

soil_ph left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the Acid band is open-ended; RHS lists pH Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no floor or ceiling can be set. NC State's prose 'lime-free soil' conflicts with RHS accepting alkaline soils.

Mature size: NC State's structured Dimensions give Height 0 ft. 9 in. - 1 ft. 0 in. (9-12 in) and Width 0 ft. 6 in. - 0 ft. 9 in. (6-9 in); RHS's description says 'to 30cm in height', consistent with that ceiling, while NC State's prose says up to 1 1/2 feet. RHS's structured Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres is a broad band, and its Max Spread 0-0.1 metre (0-3.9 in) is narrower than NC State's width. The NC State structured block is used as the anchor.
Fertilizer: NC State only says the plant benefits from bone meal or superphosphate added to the planting soil; no interval, month list or dilution strength is stated, so those fields are null.

attracts_pollinators null: NC State carries the tags th-wildlife and th-smell and fragrant flowers but no field or statement names bees, butterflies or other pollinators; RHS page shows no pollinator tag in the extracted text.
Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles and chill damage: no admissible species-specific figure; USDA zones 4a-8b (NC State) is a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature.

Cat/dog scoping: NC State supplies only Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags (no symptom list for those animals), RHS names dogs, cats, tortoises. ASPCA is not an admissible domain so its scoping is not recorded.

Edibility: is_edible is false because RHS says 'Harmful if eaten' and NC State lists poison characteristics; no source describes any part as food. NC State's symptom text spells 'salvation' (sic) for what is presumably salivation; quoted as published.
Skin contact disagreement: RHS says skin irritant with a gloves warning; NC State says Causes Contact Dermatitis: No.

records.name_note: Admissible sources reached split on the common name. NC State's dedicated page for Galanthus elwesii gives the Common Name(s) list Giant Snowdrop, Snowdrop, and its description text uses "Giant snowdrop". RHS's dedicated page renders "greater snowdrop" as its plant-profile common name beneath the H1 and lists "Elwes's snowdrop" under Other common names. Giant Snowdrop is used as the primary name, following NC State's Common Name(s) list and description text. NC State lists Chianthemum elwesii under "Previously known as". Distinct from Galanthus nivalis, which this catalog files as Common Snowdrop.
records.toxicity_detail: Two admissible sources, two scopes. RHS (Potentially harmful field): "Humans/Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten." and "Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." RHS names dogs and cats, gives no severity and names no plant part. NC State's page says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics.", tags the plant #poisonous, and its Problems field lists only "Poisonous to Humans". Its Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity Low, Poison Symptoms "CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.", Poison Toxic Principle Phenanthridine alkaloids, Causes Contact Dermatitis No, and Poison Part Roots (the only part listed). The Low rating is NC State's human-scoped rating, not a pet severity rating. NC State has no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, so the cat and dog scope comes from RHS alone. The sources differ on handling: RHS advises gloves, while NC State's human block says it does not cause contact dermatitis.
unknowns: MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org / www.missouribotanicalgarden.org) could not be reached from the sandbox (ConnectError and TLS failure), so no MoBot page for Galanthus elwesii was read. Other admissible sources (Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD, UGA) were not searched for a dedicated page on this exact taxon.

Common name: NC State leads with Giant Snowdrop, while RHS is titled 'greater snowdrop' with 'Elwes's snowdrop' as another common name. RHS lists Galanthus graecus as a synonym but not Chianthemum elwesii; NC State lists Chianthemum elwesii as 'Previously known as'. Only NC State's synonym is cited in name_note.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on RHS alone (dogs, cats: harmful if eaten, wear gloves when handling). NC State's rating is Low severity, scoped to humans, with symptoms nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. NC State's Poison Part field lists only Roots, not bulb. RHS names no part.
is_edible=false is based on RHS 'Harmful if eaten' and NC State's poison block. NC State says the toxicity is low if eaten. No source describes any edible use.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun and Partial Shade, mapped to part_shade and full_sun. RHS lists only Position Partial shade (part_shade), which is consistent. part_sun is left out because no source tags it.
direct_sun_hours_max left null. NC State's species prose says 'full sun to partial shade' with no hour figure, and the hour ranges in the Light legend are generic.

soil_drainage moderate: NC State's tags Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Wet, plus RHS 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'. soil_base garden_bed is inferred from in-ground culture (NC State soil description, landscape uses); no source labels a potting mix.
soil_ph left null. RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', and NC State lists no pH.

water_regime and the day-interval fields left null. NC State gives only soil-drainage tags (Moist, Occasionally Wet). RHS's 'does not dry out in summer' sentence is a soil-description line from the genus-level Cultivation paragraph, which can be shared with sibling snowdrop pages, so it is not used as species watering guidance. No source frames watering as a schedule for this in-ground bulb.

mature size comes from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 0 ft. 6 in. - 1 ft. 0 in.; Width 0 ft. 3 in. - 0 ft. 6 in.), converted to inches. RHS gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) and Max Spread 0-0.1 metre. RHS is wider on height and tighter on spread; NC State was used as the anchor.
chill_damage_f null: NC State's USDA zones 4a-7b and RHS's H5 rating are survival/hardiness figures, not a damage-onset temperature. NC State also notes it may be short-lived south of Zone 7.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field reads Bulb, Perennial and its USDA zones run 4a-7b; no admissible source addresses indoor culture. Temperature, humidity, light_fc, fertilizer and pH fields are null because no admissible source read addresses them for this in-ground bulb.

records.name_note: Two admissible dedicated pages lead with different names. NC State's Common Name(s) list for Lilium speciosum reads Japanese Show Lily, Rubrum Lily, Spotted Lily, alphabetized with Japanese Show Lily first. RHS's dedicated page carries a single subtitle, "showy Japanese lily", plus a separate "Other common names" list (Japanese lily, orchid lily, showy lily, spotted lily) that contains neither Japanese Show Lily nor Rubrum Lily. Japanese Show Lily was chosen because it leads NC State's Common Name(s) list; Rubrum Lily is a common alias listed on NC State's page, and NC State's description also calls the plant "the rubrum lily".
records.toxicity_detail: Cat-scoped, not dog-scoped. NC State's dedicated Lilium speciosum page has no Poison block; its prose says: "All lilies are toxic to cats from eating the leaf, licking the pollen or drinking water from a vase with lilies." Its tag block, listed together, reads: "#non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #problem for cats #showy flowers #fragrant flowers #partial shade tolerant #mass planting #full sun tolerant #bee friendly #pink flowers #butterfly friendly #edible bulbs #container plant #border", and its Problems field lists "Problem for Cats". NC State gives no symptom list and no poison-part list beyond the leaf, pollen and vase water named in that sentence. RHS's dedicated page has a "Potentially harmful" block: "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. TOXIC to pets if eaten (cats) - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". The kidney-injury statement for cats was not found on either admissible species page. Edibility conflict: NC State's tag block includes "#edible bulbs" and RHS says the bulbs are "not to be eaten", so is_edible is left null and nothing here should be read as food guidance.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant; NC State gives Plant Type Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial and USDA zones 5a-8b, and its Landscape Location list (Container, Patio, Small Space) is outdoor placement.

Cat kidney injury: neither NC State's nor RHS's Lilium speciosum page names kidney injury. NC State's sentence says 'All lilies are toxic to cats' and RHS says 'TOXIC to pets if eaten (cats)'. No dog-toxicity statement was found; NC State tags dogs as '#non-toxic for dogs'. ASPCA and vet sources are outside the admissible list, and the extension lily pages found were Easter lily or genus-level, so were not used.

is_edible left null: NC State's tag block has '#edible bulbs' while RHS says 'Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten' and both flag lilies as a cat problem. The sources disagree and neither describes a preparation.
Missouri Botanical Garden: no dedicated Lilium speciosum page was found in search, so none is cited.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the Acid band is open-ended. RHS lists only acid pH, so a ceiling from NC State's neutral band is not safe.
soil_base left null: no source states a potting versus in-ground soil recommendation in enum terms.

Mature size disagreement: NC State gives Height 4-6 ft (48-72 in) and Width 1-2 ft (12-24 in), used here. RHS (metres) gives Max Height 1-1.5 (39.4-59.1 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 (3.9-19.7 in). NC State's own description says 'up to four feet tall'.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. part_shade rests on NC State's Light field 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', RHS's Position 'Partial shade' and RHS's Cultivation 'Grow in moist, acidic soil in partial shade.' full_sun is left out: RHS's structured Position is Partial shade only and its Aspect is 'East–facing or North–facing or West–facing', with no south-facing aspect. Counterpoint: NC State's Light field also lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', its prose says 'It prefers fertile, acidic, well-drained soils and full sun.', and its tags carry '#full sun tolerant' (a tolerance tag); the same prose says 'The roots prefer cool soil, so you should plant with annuals to keep the roots shaded.'

water_regime keep_moist comes from NC State's sentence 'The soil should be moist and never dry'. RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well-drained or Poorly-drained'. NC State's structured Soil Drainage is the single value 'Good Drainage'.
Hardiness (RHS H6; NC State zones 5a-8b), chill damage, temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer and watering-interval figures: no admissible onset or cadence numbers, left null.
NC State's description says 'The roots prefer cool soil, so you should plant with annuals to keep the roots shaded'; this is not mapped to a schema field.

records.name_note: Lead name is Hardy Fuchsia, spelled with the corrected 'ch'. NC State's Common Name(s) list lists Hardy Fushia first, then Magellan Fuschia, with both names misspelled. NC State's own description prose spells it 'Hardy fuchsia'. RHS splits from NC State: its lead common name, rendered under the H1 Fuchsia magellanica, is lady's eardrops, and its Other common names field gives hummingbird fuchsia. Neither 'Hardy Fuchsia' nor NC State's 'Magellan' name appears among RHS's names. Distinct from Fuchsia × hybrida, which this catalog files as Fuchsia.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Hardy fuchsia page has no Poison block. Its only pet-related evidence is the Tags line, which reads in full: '#red flowers #nectar plant mid-summer #nectar plant late summer #window boxes #hummingbird friendly #nectar plant early fall #hanging baskets #easy to grow #fountain form #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #bee friendly #container plant #garden walls'. The cat and dog non-toxic tags are what support toxic_to_pets=false. The same NC State page's Plant Type field lists four values: Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Shrub, Vine. Edibility is a source disagreement. NC State, Fruit Description: 'Juicy oblong berries that are not edible by humans.' RHS, under its 'Potentially harmful' heading: 'Although Fuchsia berries are edible, most are not particularly tasty and are sparsely produced on plants. Fuchsia plants are generally grown as an ornamental and not for fruit crops within the UK'. The RHS sentence is genus-wording ('Fuchsia berries') on the species page and gives no symptom list, poison-part list or handling warning. NC State gives none either.
records.cool_rest_note: Dieback-to-ground, from the species page. NC State: 'generally the tops die back at the first frost', 'The roots are hardy with mulching; and in cold areas it is treated as a perennial', and 'It will die back to the ground during a hard freeze.' NC State lists USDA zones 5a-10b. RHS gives the species rating H4. These are hardiness and survival ratings, not a damage-onset temperature.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden has no dedicated Fuchsia magellanica page. Only a 'Fuchsia (group)' page and a 'Gartenmeister' cultivar page turned up, so MoBot was not used. The Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU and UMD results were genus-level or other-species pages and were not used.

Edibility conflict: NC State says the berries are 'not edible by humans', while RHS's genus-wording says 'Fuchsia berries are edible' but poor-tasting and not grown as a fruit crop. is_edible=false follows the species-specific NC State statement. Treat the RHS wording as a disclosed counterpoint, not a recommendation to eat them.
toxic_to_pets=false rests only on NC State's '#non-toxic for cats' and '#non-toxic for dogs' tags. NC State has no Poison block, and no admissible source gives a toxicity severity or symptom list.

is_houseplant is false: NC State gives Plant Type Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Shrub, Vine and USDA zones 5a-10b, and mentions hanging baskets, containers and window boxes as outdoor uses; no admissible source frames this species as a houseplant.

NC State's Dimensions block (5-10 ft height and width = 60-120 in) is the anchor. RHS gives a smaller Max Height of 1.5-2.5 m (about 59-98 in) and Max Spread of 1-1.5 m (about 39-59 in), so the sources disagree on size.

Sun: NC State's structured Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours). RHS lists Full sun and Partial shade. NC State's description prose also calls it 'shade loving' and says it does best 'with some shade'. That is prose, so full_shade is not included.
Soil pH is null. Both NC State (Acid, Alkaline and Neutral all listed) and RHS (Acid or Alkaline or Neutral) are open-ended on both sides.

water_regime is null. NC State says the plant does best in 'cool moist conditions' and RHS gives a soil Moisture field of 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'. Neither is a watering statement, so no regime is assigned. The RHS cultivation text refers to a separate 'hardy fuchsia cultivation' page and was not used.

Humidity, light in foot-candles, temperature ranges, fertilizing, watering intervals and chill-damage onset are not stated by any admissible species page. The NC State page also carries hanging-basket and container mentions, but the care guidance in this record is for the hardy in-ground shrub, not the tender hybrid basket fuchsias.

NC State lists Hardy Fuchsia's Plant Type as Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Shrub and Vine. Its Landscape Location field lists Container, Hanging Baskets and Rock Wall. Its Landscape Theme field lists Children's Garden and Water Garden.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name: RHS's plant profile leads with 'white ginger lily' as its subtitle beneath the H1 (butterfly ginger appears there only inside the longer 'white butterfly ginger lily'), while NC State's Common Name(s) list (alphabetized) and UF/IFAS's Common name(s) value both include 'butterfly ginger' first. Butterfly Ginger is used because the NC State and UF/IFAS dedicated pages lead with it. NC State also lists Hedychium coronarium var. chrysoleucum under 'Previously known as'.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox carries these tags on its Hedychium coronarium page, including the pet-safety tags: #salt tolerant #rhizomes #riparian #moist soil #showy flowers #white flowers #perennial bulbs #well-drained soil #tender bulb #heat tolerant #fall interest #humidity tolerant #wet soils tolerant #summer flowers #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #tropical feel #full sun tolerant #partial shade tolerant #container plant #fragrant flowers #edible #wetland #moth friendly. Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial. The non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs tags are NC State's pet tags; the page has no separate Poison block, no symptom list and no handling warning, and UF/IFAS FP240 makes no toxicity statement. Edibility per NC State: 'Tubers are spicy.' with the 'edible' tag; the page gives no preparation instructions, times or conditions, and says the fragrant flowers are used for garlands.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder page for this taxon (taxonid=287579) could not be loaded (proxy/connect errors); no MoBot evidence used.

No admissible readable source states regional invasive status. UF/IFAS FP240 says 'Invasive potential: not considered a problem species at this time and may be recommended by UF/IFAS faculty (reassess in 10 years)'; Hawaii/Brazil/Florida invasive listings are therefore not captured as sourced.

is_houseplant is true on UF/IFAS's Uses value 'border; mass planting; suitable for growing indoors' and NC State's 'They make excellent conservatory plants.' Both sources otherwise treat it as a garden perennial (NC State zones 7a-10b; UF/IFAS 8B-11), and NC State adds that container plants in cooler areas 'should be overwintered indoors in a greenhouse or cool, dry, frost-free location.' The research record had left this null; set at landing because the field takes true or false only.

is_edible true rests on NC State's 'Edibility: Tubers are spicy.' plus the edible tag only; no source gives preparation, dose or an edible-flower statement. Do not infer culinary use from Zingiber officinale.
soil_ph left null: RHS lists acid, alkaline and neutral; NC State has no pH field.
water_regime left null: sources give soil adjectives (moist, well-drained) not a watering statement; NC State says they do not tolerate standing water or continuously wet soil.
outdoor_sun_exposure: part_sun comes from UF/IFAS 'plant grows in part shade/part sun'; NC State's Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade map to part_shade.
Temperatures, humidity, light fc, fertilizer, chill damage: no admissible source figure. NC State hardiness zones 7a-10b and UF/IFAS 8B-11 are survival ratings, not damage onset.

Sources disagree on size. RHS gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (about 98-157 in and 39-59 in). UF/IFAS FP240 gives 'Height:  4 to 5 feet' and 'Spread:  4 to 6 feet' (48-60 in and 48-72 in). NC State's prose says stems 'grow 3 to 6 feet tall and form a clump 2 to 3 feet wide'. NC State's own structured Dimensions block (Height 4-6 ft, Width 2-3 ft) is used as the anchor; NC State is the narrowest source on spread.

NC State is internally mixed on moisture. Its prose says 'They do not tolerate standing water or continuously wet soil.', while its Soil Drainage field lists 'Occasionally Wet', its tags include '#wet soils tolerant' and '#wetland', and its Resistance To Challenges lists 'Wet Soil'. RHS Moisture reads 'Moist but well–drained' and UF lists 'occasionally wet' among its soil tolerances.

records.name_note: NC State files its page under Tibouchina urvilleana and lists Pleroma urvilleanum under a "Previously known as:" heading. RHS has a dedicated Pleroma urvilleanum page whose Name Status is Correct and whose Synonyms field lists Tibouchina urvilleana, while its separate Tibouchina urvilleana page has Name Status Synonym. Land under Pleroma urvilleanum with Tibouchina urvilleana as the synonym (the former name). On the common name the sources split. MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics says the plant is commonly called princess flower or glory bush. The UF/IFAS page title gives Princess Flower. The RHS page leads with "glory bush" as its subtitle and puts princess flower in its "Other common names" list. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Glory Bush, Princess Flower), and NC State's description opens with Princess Flower, so Princess Flower was chosen on the strength of MoBot and UF/IFAS. Glory Bush is an alias.
records.cool_rest_note: MoBot: containers should be brought indoors to a cool bright room for overwintering as houseplants before first fall frost (no temperature figure given).
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: none of the admissible pages I read (NC State, MoBot, RHS, UF/IFAS ST633) names this species as toxic or non-toxic to cats, dogs or any other animal. Clemson HGIC returned no Tibouchina page.
is_edible and attracts_pollinators are null: no admissible source addresses eating or pollinators. UF/IFAS's 'does not attract wildlife' is a fruit line, not a pollinator statement.

Invasiveness (not a schema field): MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics says it 'is now considered to be a noxious weed in Hawaii'. UF/IFAS lists its Invasive Assessment Status as 'invasive and not recommended except for specified and limited use' (High Invasion Risk, North, Central, South Florida). This is decision-relevant for recommending the plant in Hawaii and Florida.

Taxonomy: POWO (the stated accepted-name authority) is not an admissible domain, so POWO's acceptance of Pleroma urvilleanum is not cited. The support for scientific_name_accepted is RHS's dedicated Pleroma urvilleanum page (Name Status Correct). NC State still files the plant as Tibouchina urvilleana, and MoBot and UF/IFAS use Tibouchina urvilleana only.
Dedicated-page note: NC State, MoBot and UF/IFAS pages are for Tibouchina urvilleana, the same taxon under its synonym. NC State's page is the one that names Pleroma urvilleanum as the previous name.

soil_drainage = moderate: NC State's prose 'It prefers moist acidic well-drained soil.', MoBot's culture sentence 'This shrub is best grown in moist, acidic, organically rich, fertile, well-drained soils in full sun.' and RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained' all point to moist-but-well-drained. NC State's only Soil Drainage tag is 'Occasionally Wet', and MoBot's structured rows read 'Water: Medium to wet' and 'Tolerate: Wet Soil', which lean wetter. But MoBot's own 'Overly moist, water-logged soils can lead to root rot.' and UF/IFAS's 'Mushroom root rot in soil which is kept too wet.' rule out moisture_retentive. Not fast, since NC State lists occasionally wet.

water_regime and the day-interval and dry-down fields are null. No admissible source states a watering instruction for this species. NC State's and MoBot's 'moist' is a soil adjective. MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium to wet' is mid-scale and does not support keep_moist. UF/IFAS only says 'regularly watered'. RHS's 'Water freely in summer but keep just moist in winter' sits in an 'Under glass' genus-style Cultivation run that I ruled inadmissible for this field.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State's 'Acid (<6.0)' band is open-ended, and RHS lists pH as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'. MoBot says 'acidic' without a number.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's structured Light field lists both 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and its Tags row carries '#partial shade tolerant'. However, MoBot's structured Sun (Full sun), UF/IFAS's Light requirement (full sun) and RHS's Position (Full sun) all exclude part shade, so part_shade is left out. NC State's 'In hot summer areas, it likes some protection from the afternoon sun.' and MoBot's 'Prefers some afternoon shade in hot summer climates.' are conditional asides and add no value. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only maximum is NC State's site-wide legend. UF/IFAS's 'at least five hours of full sun' is a minimum for a west-facing wall.

Mature size is taken from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 6 ft. 0 in. - 8 ft. 0 in. = 72-96 in; Width 3 ft. 0 in. - 5 ft. 0 in. = 36-60 in) because that page is for this exact taxon. Other admissible sources differ. MoBot gives 6-8 ft height and 6-8 ft spread, and says it may reach 15 ft in optimum conditions. UF/IFAS gives 10-15 ft height and spread. RHS gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in) and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in) over 5-10 years. NC State's own prose says it typically reaches 6-8 ft and can reach 10-20 ft in warm winter areas.

chill_damage_f is null: sources give hardiness zones only (NC State 9a-11b; MoBot 9-11; UF/IFAS 9B-11; RHS H2), and MoBot says only that plants are 'sensitive to frost'. None states a damage-onset temperature. No source states day or night temperature ranges, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer, or active months.

is_houseplant = true rests on NC State's 'best used as an annual or house plant in zones lower than 9' and MoBot's advice to overwinter containers indoors as houseplants. It is an in-ground shrub in zones 9-11 and a container or overwintering plant elsewhere. RHS lists it as Conservatory/Greenhouse. soil_base garden_bed reflects the in-ground culture MoBot describes; a container mix is not described by any source.
RHS lists Hardiness H2 (UK ratings, not a damage-onset figure). The RHS Cultivation paragraph is not used for any field.

The audit read MoBot's rendered Common Name row as 'Common Name: princess flower' on the live page; it is not cited here because MoBot refuses this machine's quote checker, so the name_note rests on MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose instead.
